illustration.alt: Lane Kiffin stands beside a football field while an outside helper arranges five Kalshi contract cards for LSU’s playoff stages, with the championship contracts and bonus both marked $3 million.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: A third party placed five large Kalshi block trades that paid when LSU reached successive College Football Playoff milestones, offsetting bonus payments owed to Lane Kiffin; the combined championship payout was $3 million.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: LSU was effectively hedging against the cost of winning, even though winning was the valuable outcome that made the coach’s bonus worthwhile—and betting on your own games sounds more acceptable when it is called hedging.

preschool.title: LSU’s Hedge Against Winning
preschool.lesson: A third party used Kalshi contracts tied to LSU’s football success to offset Lane Kiffin’s possible bonuses, even though the victories triggering those bonuses should also benefit LSU.
paragraphs:
At Louisiana State, a prize had been planned:
Coach Lane Kiffin could earn more as his football team advanced.
Playoff, quarterfinal, semifinal, then
The championship brought bonus money again.

An outside helper tried softening the bill
With Kalshi contracts that paid when LSU did well.
Five “block trades”—large deals agreed in advance—
Covered five stages of LSU’s championship chance.

Each trade was worth $300,000 to $900,000 in size;
Together they paid $3 million for the championship prize.
That matched Kiffin’s title bonus exactly:
If LSU owed him, the contracts paid back neatly.

But winning could bring students, donations, and television pay;
That’s why LSU offered a victory bonus anyway.
The bonus costs more when the season goes right,
And costs much less after defeat ends the fight.

Once, teams betting on their games caused alarm;
Now call it “hedging,” and somehow it sounds calm.
Kalshi bans team employees from trading this way—
But if a helper trades for LSU, who is trading, anyway?

What happened? A third party helping LSU manage Lane Kiffin’s potential bonuses placed five negotiated block trades on Kalshi tied to LSU advancing through the College Football Playoff. If LSU won the national championship, the trades would pay a combined $3 million—exactly matching Kiffin’s championship bonus—even though winning itself should be financially valuable to LSU.

illustration.alt: A KPMG employee holds a confidential earnings folder beside a Polymarket yes-or-no contract while investigators approach; nearby, George Santos faces a Kalshi lifetime-ban sign.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: A KPI binary contract pays $1 if a company reaches a stated result, such as beating an earnings estimate, and $0 if it does not. An employee who trades such a contract using confidential employer information may be misappropriating that information in breach of a duty of trust.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: Prediction markets are still debating elaborate boundaries for insider trading, while Kalshi’s wonderfully blunt answer in another case was simply to ban George Santos for life.

preschool.title: The Secret-Number Bet
preschool.lesson: A KPI binary pays $1 or $0 depending on a company result; using an employer’s confidential information to buy one may be illegal because the information was entrusted to the employee.
paragraphs:
A KPI contract asks, “Did profits beat the guess?”
If yes, it pays one dollar; if not, it pays less—
in fact, it pays zero. That simple yes-or-no
can turn secret business news into valuable dough.

On Polymarket, someone from KPMG
reportedly wagered on company earnings they’d see:
Would a public company beat Wall Street’s expectation?
Authorities began an insider-trading investigation.

If the employee learned private numbers through work,
then betting with them carried a troublesome quirk:
the secret belonged to the employer, you see;
using it for personal profit could be information theft, legally.

The rules are still forming for markets like these.
Cboe says KPI bets resemble stock options; Kalshi
is overseen as a commodities exchange instead,
where hedgers may trade using facts in their head.

But Kalshi forbids those with secrets—or power
to influence an outcome—from trading that hour.
And amid all these questions of who may bet where,
Kalshi banned George Santos for life. So—there.

What happened? Authorities investigated a KPMG employee for betting on Polymarket that a specific public company would beat quarterly earnings estimates. They consider such a bet illegal if the employee used material nonpublic information entrusted to them through their job.

illustration.alt: Kim Jung-hoon turns away from a work PC that cannot install the required program, while a five-day calendar, one-hour clock, and dwindling Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix leveraged-ETF trade slips show why trading collapsed.

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: The ETFs targeted twice the chipmakers’ daily returns, while a mandatory five-day, Windows-only simulated-trading course created enough friction to deter retail investors and sharply reduce trading.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: Annoying, inconvenient software sounds like a terrible financial-stability tool, but its very unpleasantness made it effective.

preschool.title: The Windows-Only Speed Bump
preschool.lesson: South Korea reduced trading in risky 2× leveraged ETFs by requiring retail investors to complete a cumbersome five-day, Windows-only simulation before trading.
paragraphs:
On August 19, a new trading gate
made eager investors practice and wait.
For five whole days, at least one hour each,
virtual cash would help risk do its teaching.

The Windows-only program required a PC—
no quick little phone made the lesson carefree.
It covered leveraged funds linked in return
to Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix in turn.

Those funds aimed for twice each chipmaker’s daily move:
they could double a gain—or make double losses accrue.
So South Korea added some friction and fuss,
hoping a pause might protect people from loss.

Kim Jung-hoon, forty-one, lived near Seoul.
The lengthy requirement discouraged his goal.
“My work PC blocks downloads,” Kim said.
“Bring an extra laptop?” He shook his head.

“Five days and long hours? I won’t even start.
It’s too much of a hassle.” He stayed apart.
Trading value fell to four percent
of its peak back in June—a steep descent.

The funds faced their first monthly outflow as well.
The cumbersome training had worked rather well.
An annoying download, strange as could be,
was acting as a tool for financial stability.

What happened? Starting Aug. 19, South Korea required retail investors seeking certain 2× leveraged ETFs tied to Samsung Electronics Co. and SK Hynix Inc. to complete five days of Windows-only simulated trading for at least an hour per day. The hassle deterred investors, helping trading value fall to 4% of its June peak and putting the funds on course for their first monthly outflow.

illustration.alt: A government official transfers seized Anthropic share certificates once owned by Nishad Singh and Caroline Ellison to existing shareholders, with collapsed FTX boxes behind them and two coins marked “ruin” and “vast wealth.”

elementaryChecklist.financialMechanism: The three executives bought private Anthropic shares in its 2022 Series B. After FTX collapsed, Bankman-Fried’s stake was liquidated to cover claims, and the government seized Singh’s and Ellison’s shares and sold them to existing Anthropic shareholders.
elementaryChecklist.centralJoke: Their risky crypto bets landed on “ruin,” but the Anthropic shares left behind later landed on “vast wealth.”

preschool.title: The Coin That Landed Twice
preschool.lesson: When FTX collapsed, Sam Bankman-Fried’s Anthropic stake was liquidated to help repay claims, while the government seized Caroline Ellison’s and Nishad Singh’s shares and sold them to existing Anthropic shareholders; Anthropic’s later growth made those former stakes worth billions on paper.
paragraphs:
Anthropic, an AI lab concerned with keeping AI safe,
Drew effective-altruist backers fond of risk and fate.

In 2022, its Series B sold private shares to grow;
The buyers hoped their value would rise as years would go.

Sam Bankman-Fried bought $500 million—13.56 percent;
Nishad Singh put in $40 million; Caroline Ellison, $10 million spent.

Then FTX collapsed, and customers were owed;
Sam gave his Anthropic stock to help repay the load.

Bankruptcy sold Sam’s stake to settle what was due;
The government seized Singh’s and Ellison’s shares too.
It sold them to existing Anthropic owners waiting by—
A valuable survivor when the crypto bets went awry.

At a $965 billion valuation announced that May,
Those former shares were estimated in the billions anyway:
From $2.62 billion to $5.03 billion, depending who did the sums—
A fortune sprouting after FTX’s ruin comes.

The crypto coin came up “ruin” when FTX fell apart;
The Anthropic coin said “vast wealth” long after its strange start.

What happened? FTX failed, so Bankman-Fried’s Anthropic stake was liquidated, while the US government seized Singh’s and Ellison’s shares and sold them to existing Anthropic shareholders. Anthropic later became so valuable that estimates placed Singh’s and Ellison’s former stakes at $2.62 billion to $5.03 billion combined.
